why: C is the only version that tells an outside reader what 'grill Qn', 'plan review round n' and 'Dn' mean before the document leans on them; D reads smoothest of the three terse ones, B's 'This spec quotes the user's choices' is the clumsiest phrasing.

A separates the two complaints (SearXNG dependency, weak results) into labelled bullets so the reader sees the structure at once; D's 'serve the same index' is clearer than 'serve one index'; B runs everything into one paragraph and slips into present tense ('That's the state of this machine on 2026-10-22').

B introduces the 30-minute rest before defining what earns it, splits the browser-order and the config-file facts into their own bullets, gives the ranking formula its own line and says whose release zip v1.1.5 is (Consent-O-Matic's), which the others leave ambiguous; A is the densest, refers to 'the rest' before it is introduced and has an ambiguous 'never attached to it'.

A spells out the thresholds in words and moves the warm-profile, whole-run condition to the front of the block-rate sentence so it clearly scopes only that clause; B joins the two Q3 clauses with 'and' so the condition appears to govern the 95% clause too.

meaning_problems.B: Merging Q3 into one sentence makes 'over a run of the whole set, with the profile already warm' read as a condition on both the 95%-answer clause and the block-rate clause, where the others attach it to the block rate only.

C turns the stealth bullet into a sentence parallel with the other anti-goals ('web-mcp uses ...'), so it reads as the same kind of statement; A keeps a helpful comma before 'or hang past its deadline'; B and D are identical and merely list the noun phrase.

B and D (identical) name the installer as the actor that denies WebSearch/WebFetch and say 'It has no cleanup step', which ties the sentence to the installer; C adds a comma and 'has succeeded'; A's passive 'are denied' leaves the actor implicit.
A's semicolon cleanly separates the one-time skim from 'after that they are fixed'; B and C say the same with 'and'; D's 'Thresholds Q1–Q3 as proposed are fixed' is awkwardly ordered.

A alone says that `query`, `papers` and `max_passages` are parameters and that goal 8 'describes' the new ones, so a reader who hasn't memorised the tool knows what kind of things are being kept; D ends in a fragment without a comma before 'and'.

B states the rule as a full sentence ('Every engine uses a fixed English locale') and names 'the locale' as the subject of the next sentence; C opens with a fragment; D's 'queried in English' reads as the query language, which collides with the German-query sentence.

meaning_problems.D: 'Every engine is queried in English' shifts the fact from the interface locale to the language of the query, contradicting 'A query written in German still finds German pages'.

why: A writes every constraint as a sentence and makes the parser rule's reasoning explicit ('read what other tools write, so, by CLAUDE.md's rule, they test against captured pages'); C and D are nearly as clear but keep a terse 'Installer:' label; B is telegraphic fragments throughout.
